text: a quick visual analysis of why this Converse ad is so disturbing. The first thing that people notice is that this looks like someone hanging and the way that the light is hitting the skirt looks like a Klan hood but the rest of the skirt too looks like a Klan robe. From that perspective these shoes on the outside begin to look like a lynch mob and then this star which is part of the Converse logo begins to look like a confederate star. So was this Converse ad secretly showing a KKK hood and the lynching or did the internet turn a pair of sneakers into a conspiracy theory? If you've been on social media this past week you've probably seen the controversy around Converse ad. Some people say Converse intentionally published a racist image, others say people are seeing things that simply aren't there. I wanted to look into what actually happened but it appeared to be more difficult than I thought. Converse has since removed the disputed images and posts so it is pretty difficult to reconstruct the timeline of events. So what comes next is my best effort. It all started around June 29th when Converse announced K-pop star Karina as a global ambassador and introduced the Chuk70x. The shoes were already available in Korea and China before its wider release on August 27th. The campaign included a video and full frame photos of Karina that didn't have much controversies around them and for about two months it was simply an ad. But then around September 3rd something changed. Someone from Converse had a genius idea to post a cropped image from that campaign on threads. At first that post also appears to have attracted little attention but around September 17th it spread widely and people began pointing out what they saw. The triangular light on the white skirt looked to some like a KKK hood. The black shoes hanging beside it looked to some like the feet of a person being lynched. And hey, I can see why that reading would be upsetting. Once somebody points it out, it is difficult to unsee. Converse eventually removed the image and apologized saying it understood why people found it deeply upsetting and that it had got it wrong. But the question of whether it was an intentional racism still remained. I can't know what everyone involved was thinking but based on what we can actually see, I don't think there's good evidence for deliberate racist message. First, look at the full campaign. You can see Karina holding the shoes. She is the subject of the photograph standing in a Converse star. That gives the supposedly sinister shapes an ordinary explanation. If this were meant to depict a KKK scene, why make that scene disappear as soon as you show the rest of the ad? Moreover, why having a K-pop star instead of some white man? Second, think about the company's incentives. Converse and Jordan brand are part of Nike, a publicly traded company. Nike and its brands have committed substantial money to organizations addressing racial inequality, and Converse has funded its own Black Joy projects. Deliberately slipping KKK imagery into a global campaign would be shooting itself in the foot. Third, think about their customers. Nike, Jordan brand, and Converse have deep ties to basketball and black sneaker culture. Across those brands, millions of black people wear their shoes. Why would Converse deliberately put KKK imagery in an ad and alienate those customers? It makes no commercial sense. Fourth, Converse took down the image, acknowledged why people found it upsetting, and apologized. An apology cannot tell us what was in someone's head, but it does show that the company didn't stand behind the image once the problem was raised. And I'm sure you can come up with plenty of other reasons why would it make close to zero sense for Converse to intentionally send a racist message. So unless Converse decided to lynch itself with its own ads, this looks to me like a genuine marketing mistake. And you can decide for yourself whether the reaction was justified or whether some people overreacted.
